query: What are feasible minimum specimen dimensions and FIB time/cost estimates for SE(B) and micro‑cantilever fracture tests, and alternates when sampling is prohibited?

response.query: What are feasible minimum specimen dimensions and FIB time/cost estimates for SE(B) and micro‑cantilever fracture tests, and alternates when sampling is prohibited?
response.answer: Minimum specimen dimensions for SE(B) and micro-cantilever tests are typically small, often less than 1 mm. FIB time/cost is variable but generally expensive; alternatives include micro-casting and nanoindentation when sampling is prohibited.

results.title: Specimen Dimension - an overview
results.content: However, as discussed earlier in this manuscript, according to ASTM D1621, the minimum specimen geometry is typically not attainable when utilizing most dynamic testing apparatuses such as SHPBs. Therefore, research work has been done on the subject to find the minimum acceptable specimen size in the dynamic testing of foam materials. [256] investigated the effect of specimen size on the stress/strain response regarding the ratio of the smallest specimen dimension to the foam cell size. For example, Cronin and Ouellet [34] investigated the foam specimen size effect by considering three different cylindrical sample sizes (diameters of 10 mm, 17 mm and 35 mm at a constant height). [87] investigated the size effect at the quasi-static regime as they were not able to test larger specimens at higher strain rates using their SHPB apparatus. [57] work on PU foams' rate sensitivity can clearly demonstrate the problem with reporting the strain rate sensitivity versus the nominal strain rate without considering the specimen size effect. The foam mechanical responses at strain rates of 10 s−1 to 100 s−1 were investigated by testing specimens with a thickness of 24.5 mm employing a droptower apparatus. As shown in Table 4, polymeric foam specimens with thicknesses of 2.5 mm [96] to 100 mm [153] have been used in the experimental investigations of the polymeric foam's rate sensitivity, and results were often reported based on the nominal strain rates. ### 4.1 Effect of testing and specimen dimensions on mechanical properties of ECC The mechanical properties of ECC are affected mainly based on three parameters such as shape, size and loading conditions or friction of the specimen. Although, it was observed that the testing and specimen dimensions are not much affected the mechanical properties of ECC compared to the effect of the influence of materials, mixing ratios and curing conditions. ### 5.3 Effect of size of specimen and notch/depth ratio on fracture energy The most significant issue besides crack propagation, is the effect of size. Therefore, prior to specimen tests of fracture mechanics, tensile beam tests have shown that with increasing size, tensile strength is reduced and then the materials tend to have a brittle behavior [2,157–159]. Specimen size is also effective in different methods of measuring fracture energy.

results.content: + In-situ SEM micromechanical testing. - Simultaneous Mechanical Testing with STEM/EBSD. + In-situ SEM micromechanical testing. - Simultaneous Mechanical Testing with STEM/EBSD. Simultaneous Mechanical Testing with STEM/EBSD. # Micro-Tensile Testing. Conventional tensile testing is the gold standard for measuring the yield, ultimate, and fracture strength and ductility of materials. However, while these tests provide valuable insights into the work hardening behavior and overall material properties, they average out the effects of each constituents, such as the different phases or interfaces. For this, micro-tensile testing is required. For sample preparation, focused ion beam (FIB) machining can be used to create dog-bone shaped samples with a uniform cross-section that remain attached to the original substrate. This gripper shape enables the interlocking with the dog bone sample in order to conduct micro-tensile tests. ## Application Examples. * 01 Micro-Cast Tensile Samples. ### FIB-Free Alternatives for Micro-tensile Testing Sample Fabrication. Focused Ion Beam (FIB) can produce samples with great control over location and geometric dimensions. In this application example, silver wires were micro-cast using a silicon mold, then tested using in-situ micro-tension at room temperature, 200 °C, and 400 °C in displacement control. In this application example, a nanocrystalline Cu-Zr alloy was developed that provides increased ductility achieved by engineering the grain boundaries to have a high degree of structural disorder. Micro-tensile testing showed that samples with Amorphous Intergranular Films (AIF) exhibited a 44% increase in tensile ductility. Metallic Glasses (MGs) have sparked interest for their superior properties, including high elastic strain limits and strength, compared to crystalline materials. Despite their potential in micromechanical applications, the effect of size on their properties is not fully understood. In this application example, the creep behavior of metallic glass nanowires was investigated by attaching them between an FT-S Microforce Sensing Probe and a secondary substrate using Platinum-Electron Beam Induced Deposition (Pt-EBID). Creep tests were conducted at various temperatures by gradually increasing the nanowire temperature with electric current, offering insights into how temperature affects their mechanical behavior and advancing our understanding of size effects on material properties. ## More Applications. ### **Nanoindentation**. ### **Micro-Cantilever Testing**. ### **High-Temperature Testing**. ### **Scratch Testing**. ### **Simultaneous Mechanical Testing with STEM/EBSD**. ## Nanoindentation Revolutionized: Unleashing the Power of Tomorrow's Technology.

Comparing the interfacial fracture energy of the Cu-SiOx interface from the DCB tests to literature, we find that the values can range from 0.6 to 100 J/m2,13 strongly depending on the film thickness that spanned from 40 to 3000 nm. results.title: Double-Cantilever Beam - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: A double cantilever beam (DCB) is defined as a rectangular bar with a slit that is subjected to symmetrical opening tensile loads at its ends, enabling the study of crack growth rates under tensile opening mode (Mode I). The double cantilever beam (DCB) specimen, shown in Fig. 5.3, is the most widely used specimen for the measurement of mode I interlaminar fracture toughness. This is accounted for by using the modified beam theory method of data reduction, in which the DCB specimen is treated as if it had a longer crack length:. The DCB is a useful joint for studying crack propagation and to estimate the fatigue constants appearing in the Paris law, since the test coupons are simple to fabricate and the available analytical methods such as beam theories are well established (the most relevant ones are described later in Section 4.5.1). Otherwise, measurement errors of the crack length (*a*) can reduce the measurement accuracy of the critical strain energy release rate or fracture toughness (generally *G*c; *G*Ic or *G*IIc for mode I or II components, respectively). While the test is being performed, a video camera is recording the crack length on the side of the composite specimen. The double cantilever beam (DCB) test is the most commonly used method for measuring the initiation and propagation values of Mode I fracture energy GI under static and cyclic loading conditions (see ASTM D3433, BS 7991 and ISO 25217). The tapered double cantilever beam (TDCB) test geometry (Fig. 6.18) ensures that the change in compliance is independent of the crack length (i.e. constant compliance). The TDCB test specimen has been used to determine the rate of crack growth under various cyclic loading and environmental conditions. These can take the form of double cantilever beam (DCB), end notched flexure (ENF), end loaded split (ELS) and mixed mode bending (MMB) tests amongst others.29 It is tests such as these that have been used to develop and validate the numerical formulations described above and investigate such effects as variation in maximum stress, traction displacement shape and mesh size.
